value.overview: The Tawny-winged Woodcreeper (Dendrocincla anabatina) is a small forest woodcreeper of Central America. It climbs trunks and large branches while searching bark, crevices, foliage, and leaf litter for invertebrates. Its plumage is mostly warm brown, with noticeably tawny wings and a relatively plain appearance compared with many streaked woodcreepers. In Costa Rica it is a resident species of humid lowland and foothill forests, where it is usually found singly or in pairs and can be unobtrusive.
value.classification: The species belongs to the woodcreeper subfamily Dendrocolaptinae within the ovenbird family Furnariidae. It is placed in the genus Dendrocincla, a group of mostly forest-dwelling woodcreepers.
value.identification: This is a small to medium-sized woodcreeper with a slim, slightly decurved bill, stiff tail, and upright trunk-climbing posture. The upperparts are warm brown, while the wings and wing coverts have a distinct tawny or rufous tone that gives the species its common name. The underparts are generally buffy to brownish, with limited fine streaking compared with several similar woodcreepers. Identification is aided by its compact shape, plain facial pattern, and habit of moving methodically along trunks and larger limbs.
value.rangeHabitat: The Tawny-winged Woodcreeper ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and western Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in humid Caribbean-slope and southern Pacific forests, including lowlands and foothills, and has also been recorded at sites such as Los Cusingos. It uses mature evergreen forest, older secondary woodland, forest edges, and other wooded habitats with substantial trees and climbing surfaces. It is generally associated with moist forest rather than open agricultural landscapes.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout most or all of its range. It is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of this species is not as well documented as that of many more familiar Central American birds. Like other woodcreepers, it is believed to nest in a cavity or sheltered natural opening in a tree, using a simple nest arrangement of plant material or other soft debris. Breeding activity is associated with the local wet-season or early rainy-season period in parts of its range, but timing can vary geographically. The species is normally encountered singly or in pairs during the breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists chiefly of arthropods, including beetles, ants, termites, spiders, and other insects. It forages by climbing tree trunks and thick branches, probing bark crevices and inspecting epiphytes, moss, and nearby foliage. It may also take prey from the ground or leaf litter. The Tawny-winged Woodcreeper can join mixed-species feeding flocks and may investigate areas where army ants disturb hidden invertebrates, but it is not considered one of the most specialized army-ant-following woodcreepers.
value.behavior: This woodcreeper is usually quiet and inconspicuous, moving with short hops up trunks and along branches while bracing itself with its stiff tail. It often forages alone or in pairs, though it may associate with mixed forest flocks. Its brown plumage provides effective camouflage in shaded woodland. When disturbed, it commonly slips to the far side of a trunk or moves into dense vegetation rather than flying into the open. Vocal activity is most noticeable during territorial and breeding interactions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not known to be undergoing a rapid decline, but a precise population estimate and detailed long-term trend are unavailable.
